pages.title: A obra e a situação

work.title: Five Little Peppers and How They Grew
work.note: Five Little Peppers and How They Grew é um livro infantil publicado em 1881 por Margaret Sidney, pseudônimo de uma autora americana. Conta a vida de uma viúva pobre que sustenta cinco filhos numa casinha simples. Apesar da falta de dinheiro, a família se ajuda, inventa alegrias e vive unida em meio às pequenas aventuras do dia a dia. A aula retorna à obra para explorar “mandar lembranças com Say hi to… e Give my love

facts.sub: Nos EUA, famílias separadas por distância costumam combinar um dia e uma hora fixos para ligar. É comum começar com “Can you see me?” e “Can you hear me?”, antes de qualquer conversa longa.

facts.label: Microfone desligado
facts.sub: Em muitas chamadas, alguém fala e ninguém ouve, porque o microfone está desligado. O aviso comum é “You’re on mute”. A pessoa clica no ícone, diz “Sorry!” e repete o que falou.

pages.title: Mito ou fato? · 1/2

items.s: On a video call, it is normal to ask, “Can you hear me?”
items.why: Sound problems are common, so people check early.

items.s: You cannot talk if you see “You’re on mute.”
items.why: It only means your microphone is off. Turn it on and talk.

items.s: People often say “Talk soon” at the end of a call.
items.why: It is a friendly, short goodbye.

answers: On a video call, it is normal to ask, “Can you hear me?” → Verdadeiro (Sound problems are common, so people check early.)

People often say “Talk soon” at the end of a call. → Verdadeiro (It is a friendly, short goodbye.)

pages.title: Can you hear me? · 1/2
paragraphs: Ruth lives in a new apartment in Dayton. It is winter, and it is cold outside. Her mom is far away, so Ruth makes a **video call**. She sits on the sofa and opens her laptop. The screen is bright, and she smiles. She waits for her mom to answer the call.

“**Hi, Mom! Can you see me?**” “**Hi, honey! Yes, I can see you!**” “**Can you hear me?**” “**A little. Turn up the volume.**” Ruth clicks the button. “**Better now?**” “**Yes, perfect. How are you?**”

pages.title: Can you hear me? · 2/2
paragraphs: “**I’m great. I love my new place.**” “**Show me your apartment!**” “**Okay. This is my living room.**” Ruth turns the camera. Her mom sees a sofa, a window and a green plant. Mom smiles, and her eyes get wet.

Ruth thinks about a book, “Five Little Peppers.” A poor mother and her five children stay close with love, not money. Ruth has a family like that. “**Miss you**,” she says. “**Love you. Talk soon.**” Mom starts to answer, but Ruth hears nothing. “Oh no,” Mom says, “**you’re on mute!**” They both laugh.

items.why: Use Can + you + base verb. Do not use -ing with hear.
Use can’t + see, and well, not good, for how you see.
Turn up is a phrasal verb, with no to.
Use the simple present for feelings: I miss you.
